slides.say: Some motion questions need almost no calculation. We only need ratios, the same way and opposite ways.

slides: Ratios run through the whole quantitative section. And in motion, they save a lot of work.

slides.say: These rules are just like the ones in work and rate. First, when the time is fixed, the speed and the distance go the same way.
Say I have one hour to run. At eight kilometers per hour, I cover eight kilometers.
At twelve kilometers per hour, I cover twelve kilometers. The faster I run, the farther I get.
Eight to twelve is two to three. So if the speeds are two to three, the distances are two to three too.
at: if the speeds are two to three

slides.say: Second, when the speed is fixed, the time and the distance go the same way too.
I run at ten kilometers per hour. In one hour I cover ten kilometers. In two hours, twenty.
at: I run at ten kilometers per hour

slides.say: In three hours, thirty. The more time I have, the farther I get.
Third, when the distance is fixed, the speed and the time go opposite ways. This is where students slip.
From my house to a friend's house is twelve kilometers. At four kilometers per hour, twelve divided by four is three hours.
At six kilometers per hour, twelve divided by six is two hours. The faster I go, the less time it takes.
The speeds are four to six, that's two to three. And the times are three to two. The ratio flips.
Why does it flip? Because the speed times the time must stay twelve. Four times three is twelve, and six times two is twelve.
So the real skill is to spot when to use these rules. Before we use a rule, we ask, what is fixed here? The time, the speed, or the distance?
Let's try four quick situations. Two cars drive the same three hours. The time is fixed, so the distances follow the speeds.
at: Two cars drive the same three hours

slides.say: Someone drives to a town and back on the same road. The distance is fixed, so the times flip.
Two people start together and stop together, when they meet. The time is fixed, so the distances follow the speeds.
A train keeps the same speed all day. The speed is fixed, so more time means more distance. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
at: A train keeps the same speed
